sections.heading: Physical quantities and units
paragraphs: Physics describes matter, energy and natural phenomena using observation, measurement and mathematical models. A physical quantity is expressed as a numerical value multiplied by a unit. Fundamental quantities are independent; derived quantities are built from them.

sections.heading: SI base quantities
bullets: Length: metre (m); mass: kilogram (kg); time: second (s).
Electric current: ampere (A); thermodynamic temperature: kelvin (K); amount of substance: mole (mol); luminous intensity: candela (cd).
Examples of derived units: speed m/s, acceleration m/s², force newton N = kg·m/s², energy joule J = N·m, pressure pascal Pa = N/m².
Metric prefixes represent powers of ten: kilo 10³, centi 10⁻², milli 10⁻³, micro 10⁻⁶, nano 10⁻⁹. Apply the exponent to the unit as well as the value when converting areas and volumes.

sections.heading: Dimensional analysis and conversion
bullets: Multiply by conversion factors equal to 1, arranged so unwanted units cancel. Example: 72 km/h × (1000 m/1 km) × (1 h/3600 s) = 20 m/s.
For area, square the length conversion factor; for volume, cube it. Thus 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m² and 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³.
Check that both sides of a physical equation have the same dimensions. Dimensional consistency can expose errors, though it cannot prove an equation is physically correct.
Keep units through each calculation and round only at the end.

sections.heading: Uncertainty and significant digits
bullets: No measurement is perfectly exact. Report a measured value with appropriate precision and, where available, its uncertainty.

Significant digits communicate measurement precision. Nonzero digits count; leading zeros do not; zeros between nonzero digits count; trailing zeros count when a decimal point makes the precision clear.
For multiplication and division, the result generally has no more significant figures than the least precise input. For addition and subtraction, round to the least precise decimal place.

Distinguish accuracy (closeness to the accepted value) from precision (repeatability or fineness of resolution). Repeated readings can reveal random variation; calibration errors can create systematic bias.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Convert quantities with unit cancellation shown at every step.
Identify the base units inside a derived unit and check dimensions in equations.
Round only after calculation and explain how the measurement precision determines the final digits.

sections.heading: Scalar and vector quantities
bullets: A scalar has magnitude only (for example mass, time, temperature or energy). A vector has magnitude and direction (for example displacement, velocity, acceleration or force).
Represent a vector by an arrow: length gives magnitude and arrowhead gives direction. The negative vector has the same magnitude and opposite direction.
Vector addition obeys the triangle or head-to-tail method. The parallelogram method gives the same resultant for two vectors applied from a common point.

sections.heading: Components and unit vectors
bullets: Resolve a vector A of magnitude A at angle θ from +x into Ax=A cos θ and Ay=A sin θ. Use the stated angle reference and signs to identify the correct quadrant.
In two dimensions, A = Ax î + Ay ĵ. Its magnitude is |A|=√(Ax²+Ay²), and its direction is recovered from tan θ=Ay/Ax with quadrant adjustment.
Add vectors by adding corresponding components: Rx=ΣAx and Ry=ΣAy; then R=√(Rx²+Ry²). This method handles several vectors cleanly.
A unit vector has magnitude one and points in a specified direction. For nonzero A, its unit vector is Â=A/|A|.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Draw a coordinate sketch before resolving vectors and mark the angle reference.
Use algebraic signs for components; do not add magnitudes when directions differ.
After finding components, report both resultant magnitude and direction with units where applicable.

units.title: Chapter 2 - Kinematics and Dynamics of Particles

topics.title: Motion in one and two dimensions

sections.heading: Position, displacement, velocity and acceleration
bullets: Position describes location relative to an origin. Displacement Δx=x_f−x_i is a signed change in position; distance is total path length and is never negative.
Average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time; average speed is distance divided by elapsed time. Instantaneous velocity is the rate of change of position.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. It points in the direction of velocity change, which can differ from the direction of motion when an object slows down.
In two dimensions, treat x and y components independently while using the same time interval. Recombine components for velocity or displacement magnitude and direction.

sections.heading: Constant-acceleration equations
bullets: For constant acceleration: v=v₀+at; x=x₀+v₀t+½at²; v²=v₀²+2a(x−x₀); and Δx=½(v₀+v)t.
Choose a coordinate direction and keep signs consistent. These equations apply only when acceleration is constant.
Free fall is motion under gravity alone (neglecting air resistance). Near Earth, acceleration has magnitude g≈9.8 m/s² downward; its algebraic sign depends on the chosen positive direction.
At the top of a vertical throw, instantaneous vertical velocity is zero but acceleration remains downward at g.

sections.heading: Projectile motion
bullets: Ideal projectile motion neglects air resistance: horizontal acceleration is zero and vertical acceleration is −g for upward-positive coordinates.
Resolve launch velocity: v₀x=v₀ cos θ and v₀y=v₀ sin θ. Then x=x₀+v₀x t and y=y₀+v₀y t−½gt².

For launch and landing at the same height, time of flight T=2v₀ sin θ/g, maximum height H=v₀² sin²θ/(2g), and range R=v₀² sin(2θ)/g. Use these special formulas only when launch and landing elevations match.
The horizontal and vertical motions share the same time. Solve the coordinate equation that gives the needed time, then substitute into the other coordinate.

sections.heading: Exam problem strategy
bullets: List known and unknown quantities, draw axes, define positive directions, and select an equation matching the conditions.
For a graph, slope of position-time gives velocity; slope of velocity-time gives acceleration; area under velocity-time gives displacement.
Check limiting cases and units. A negative component indicates direction, not a negative magnitude.

sections.heading: Forces and Newton’s laws
bullets: A force is an interaction that can change motion; force is a vector measured in newtons. Common forces include weight, normal force, tension, friction, spring force and applied force.
Newton’s first law: an object maintains rest or constant velocity unless a net external force acts. Inertia is resistance to change in motion.
Newton’s second law: ΣF=ma. Apply it to each object using a free-body diagram containing only forces acting on that object.
Newton’s third law: interaction forces occur in equal-magnitude, opposite-direction pairs on different bodies; they therefore do not cancel on one free-body diagram.
Weight near Earth is W=mg downward. Normal force is perpendicular to the contact surface and is not automatically equal to mg; determine it from the force balance.
For kinetic friction, f_k=μ_k N; static friction adjusts up to f_s≤μ_s N. A spring obeys Hooke’s law F=−kx within its elastic range.

sections.heading: Uniform circular motion
bullets: An object moving at constant speed in a circle still accelerates because its velocity direction changes. Centripetal acceleration points toward the center: a_c=v²/r=ω²r.
Required inward net force is ΣF_radial=mv²/r. ‘Centripetal force’ names the net inward force; it is supplied by actual forces such as tension, friction or gravity.
Period T is time per revolution, frequency f=1/T, angular speed ω=2π/T=2πf, and tangential speed v=ωr.

sections.heading: Universal gravitation and planetary motion
bullets: Two masses attract with F=Gm₁m₂/r² along the line joining their centers. G is the universal gravitational constant and r is center-to-center separation.
Near a spherical planet of mass M, g=GM/r²; gravitational field strength decreases with distance from the center. Weight depends on local g, while mass is intrinsic.
Kepler’s laws: planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus; the Sun-planet radius sweeps equal areas in equal times; and T² is proportional to a³ for bodies orbiting the same central mass.
Satellites remain in orbit because gravity supplies centripetal acceleration. Apparent weightlessness in orbit is continuous free fall, not absence of gravity.

sections.heading: Exam problem strategy
bullets: Draw a separate free-body diagram and choose axes aligned with motion or acceleration.
Resolve inclined forces into components before applying ΣF=ma; include only real forces on the diagram.
For orbit questions, distinguish radius from altitude: r=planet radius+height above surface.

topics.title: Work, energy, momentum and center of mass

sections.heading: Work, kinetic energy and conservation
bullets: Work by a constant force is W=F d cos θ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement. Work is positive when force helps displacement, negative when it opposes, and zero when perpendicular.
Kinetic energy K=½mv². The work-energy theorem states net work equals change in kinetic energy: W_net=ΔK.
Near Earth, gravitational potential energy U_g=mgy relative to a chosen reference level; spring potential energy U_s=½kx².
For a system with only conservative forces, mechanical energy K+U is conserved. Nonconservative work changes mechanical energy: W_nc=Δ(K+U). Choose a reference level consistently.

sections.heading: Power and momentum
bullets: Power is the rate of doing work: average P=W/Δt; instantaneous P=F·v. SI unit is watt (W).
Linear momentum p=mv. Impulse J=F_avg Δt=Δp; force over time changes momentum.
For an isolated system, total momentum is conserved when net external impulse is zero. Analyze all interacting bodies together.

sections.heading: Collisions and center of mass
bullets: In every isolated collision, total momentum is conserved. In an elastic collision, kinetic energy is also conserved; in an inelastic collision, some kinetic energy becomes other forms.
A perfectly inelastic collision is one in which bodies stick together after impact. Use momentum conservation to find their shared final velocity; do not conserve kinetic energy in this case.
For particles on a line, center of mass x_cm=Σm_i x_i/Σm_i; in two dimensions apply the same weighted average separately to x and y.
The center of mass moves as if the system’s total mass were concentrated there and the net external force acted on it: ΣF_ext=M a_cm.

sections.heading: Exam problem strategy
bullets: Choose energy methods when forces are complicated but initial and final states are clear; choose momentum for short collisions or interactions.
Define the system and direction before applying conservation. Momentum is a signed vector quantity.
Track energy forms and state whether external work or nonconservative forces are present.

sections.heading: Properties of matter
bullets: Density ρ=m/V measures mass per unit volume. Specific gravity is the ratio of a substance’s density to a reference density and has no units.
Stress is force per area; strain is fractional change in dimension. Elastic response returns toward the original shape when the load is removed, within the elastic limit.
Pressure is normal force per area: P=F/A, measured in pascals (Pa). A fluid at rest exerts pressure in all directions and pressure acts perpendicular to a surface.

sections.heading: Pressure in static fluids
bullets: At depth h below a fluid surface open to the atmosphere, absolute pressure P=P₀+ρgh; gauge pressure is ρgh. Pressure increases with density and depth, not with container shape.
Pascal’s principle: a pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted throughout the fluid. Hydraulic systems trade force for displacement: F₁/A₁=F₂/A₂ in ideal conditions.
When comparing points in a connected static fluid, pressure is equal at the same height within the same continuous fluid; use pressure differences to avoid unnecessary atmospheric terms.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Convert area carefully in pressure calculations and express the final result in Pa or an equivalent unit.
Separate absolute pressure from gauge pressure and identify the reference surface.
For hydraulic devices, relate force to piston area through equal pressure, not equal force.

sections.heading: Buoyant force and Archimedes’ principle
bullets: A fluid exerts an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of displaced fluid: F_B=ρ_fluid V_displaced g.
An object floats when buoyant force balances its weight. For a floating object, the displaced-fluid weight equals the object’s weight; only the submerged volume contributes to displacement.
Apparent weight while immersed is reduced by buoyancy: W_app=mg−F_B, provided the object is supported or suspended as described.
Whether an object sinks or floats depends on its average density relative to the fluid, together with the displaced volume available.

sections.heading: Continuity and Bernoulli equation
bullets: For steady incompressible flow, volume flow rate Q=Av is constant along a pipe: A₁v₁=A₂v₂. A narrower section has higher flow speed.
Bernoulli’s equation for ideal steady flow along a streamline is P+½ρv²+ρgy=constant. Its terms represent pressure, kinetic energy per volume and gravitational potential energy per volume.
At equal heights, higher fluid speed corresponds to lower static pressure in this ideal-flow model. Apply Bernoulli only under its assumptions and compare points along the same streamline.
Viscosity, turbulence and pumps can cause real-flow behavior to depart from the ideal model; include them when specified.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Identify the displaced volume for buoyancy, not automatically the object’s full volume.
Use continuity before Bernoulli when pipe areas differ.
Keep pressure, speed and height terms in consistent SI units and compare the same two points.

sections.heading: Temperature and thermal equilibrium
bullets: Temperature describes thermal state and determines the direction of spontaneous heat transfer: heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature.
Zeroth law: if systems A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with system C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This supports the use of thermometers.
Convert temperature scales carefully: T(K)=T(°C)+273.15; °F=(9/5)°C+32. Temperature differences in kelvins and Celsius degrees have equal numerical size.

sections.heading: Thermal expansion
bullets: For small temperature changes, linear expansion ΔL=αL₀ΔT, where α is the linear expansion coefficient.
Area expansion is approximately ΔA=βA₀ΔT with β≈2α; volume expansion ΔV=γV₀ΔT with γ≈3α for isotropic solids.
Expansion joints and bimetallic strips use differential expansion. In constrained materials, expansion can create stress; do not assume an object is free to expand if the problem says it is fixed.

sections.heading: Heat, specific heat and phase changes
bullets: Heat is energy transferred because of temperature difference; it is not a substance stored in an object. Internal energy is microscopic energy within a system.
For temperature change without phase change, Q=mcΔT, where c is specific heat capacity. A high c means more energy is needed for the same mass and temperature change.
During a phase change at constant temperature, Q=mL, where L is the latent heat for that phase transition.
In calorimetry, energy conservation gives heat lost + heat gained = 0 for an insulated system. Include phase changes and use each material’s mass and heat capacity separately.

sections.heading: Heat transfer
bullets: Conduction transfers energy through material interactions, especially in solids; the rate depends on conductivity, area, thickness and temperature difference.
Convection transfers heat through bulk fluid motion, driven naturally by density differences or by external circulation.
Thermal radiation transfers energy by electromagnetic waves and does not require a material medium; hotter surfaces generally radiate more energy.
More than one transfer mechanism can act at once. Identify the physical path rather than treating all heat transfer as conduction.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Use kelvins in thermodynamic relations that require absolute temperature.
Separate sensible heating (mcΔT) from latent heat (mL) when a phase change occurs.
Draw an energy balance and define which objects gain or lose heat before solving.

topics.title: Work, internal energy and the first law

sections.heading: Thermodynamic systems and work
bullets: A system is the matter or region under study; its surroundings are everything else. A closed system exchanges energy but not matter with its surroundings.
Work is energy transfer by an organized macroscopic force or process; heat is transfer driven by temperature difference. Sign conventions must be stated.
For gas expansion at constant pressure, work done by the gas is W=PΔV. Expansion gives positive work by the gas; compression gives negative work by the gas.

sections.heading: First law of thermodynamics
bullets: The first law is energy conservation applied to thermal systems. With W_by as work done by the system: ΔU=Q−W_by.
If instead W_on means work done on the system, the equivalent form is ΔU=Q+W_on. Do not mix sign conventions within one calculation.
Positive Q adds energy to the system; positive work done by the system transfers energy out as work. Use the problem’s stated convention if it differs.
For a complete cycle, the system returns to its initial state so ΔU=0; net heat input equals net work done by the system under this convention.

sections.heading: Exam problem strategy
bullets: Define the system and sign convention before substituting values.
Check units: joules for heat, work and internal-energy change; pascals times cubic metres also gives joules.
Explain the physical meaning of the sign of ΔU, Q and W rather than reporting numbers alone.

sections.heading: Periodic motion and SHM
bullets: Periodic motion repeats after period T; frequency f=1/T is cycles per second (hertz). Angular frequency ω=2πf=2π/T.
Simple harmonic motion occurs when restoring acceleration is proportional to displacement and points toward equilibrium: a=−ω²x.
For x(t)=A cos(ωt+φ), amplitude A is maximum displacement, phase φ sets the initial state, velocity is the time derivative and acceleration is −ω²x.

Maximum speed is v_max=ωA at equilibrium; maximum acceleration is a_max=ω²A at the endpoints. Kinetic and potential energy exchange while total mechanical energy remains constant in an ideal oscillator.

sections.heading: Mass-spring system and simple pendulum
bullets: For an ideal mass-spring oscillator, ω=√(k/m) and T=2π√(m/k). A stiffer spring gives a shorter period; a larger mass gives a longer period.
For a simple pendulum at small angular displacement, T=2π√(L/g). The period depends on length and local g, and is approximately independent of mass and amplitude only for small swings.
Use the equilibrium position as x=0 and choose a consistent phase when writing position, velocity and acceleration equations.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Convert frequency to period or angular frequency before using SHM equations.
At equilibrium, speed is greatest and restoring acceleration is zero; at endpoints, speed is zero and acceleration magnitude is greatest.
State the small-angle assumption when applying the pendulum period formula.

topics.title: Waves, resonance, Doppler effect and image formation

sections.heading: Wave characteristics
bullets: A wave transfers energy and disturbance; in a mechanical wave, the medium oscillates but does not travel with the wave as a whole.
Wavelength λ is distance between points in the same phase; frequency f is oscillations per second; wave speed v=fλ.
Transverse oscillations are perpendicular to travel direction; longitudinal oscillations are parallel. Amplitude measures maximum disturbance.
In a fixed medium, wave speed is determined by medium properties; changing frequency changes wavelength accordingly.

sections.heading: Resonance and Doppler effect
bullets: Resonance occurs when a periodic driving frequency is near a system’s natural frequency, producing a large response when damping is low.
The Doppler effect is an observed frequency shift caused by relative motion between source and observer. Approach raises observed frequency; recession lowers it.
Use the Doppler equation with a declared sign convention for source and observer velocities; distinguish motion of the medium from motion through the medium when relevant.

sections.heading: Mirrors, thin lenses and ray diagrams
bullets: For spherical mirrors and thin lenses, the module uses the imaging relation 1/f=1/d_o+1/d_i, with sign conventions determining whether image distance is real or virtual.
Magnification m=h_i/h_o=−d_i/d_o under the common sign convention. A negative sign indicates inversion; |m| gives relative image size.
Converging lenses and concave mirrors can form real or virtual images depending on object distance; diverging lenses and convex mirrors form virtual, upright, reduced images for real objects.

Use principal rays: parallel rays reflect/refract through (or appear to diverge from) the focal point; a ray through the optical center of a thin lens continues approximately straight; a ray through the mirror center of curvature retraces its path.
Draw a labeled ray diagram to check whether image orientation, size and real/virtual classification agree with the calculated signs.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Relate wave speed, frequency and wavelength with consistent units.
Identify whether the source and observer approach or recede before applying Doppler signs.
Keep the optics sign convention consistent and verify a numerical result with a ray sketch.

sections.heading: Charge and Coulomb’s law
bullets: Electric charge is positive or negative, measured in coulombs; like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Charge is conserved and quantized in multiples of the elementary charge.
Coulomb’s law for point charges: F=k|q₁q₂|/r² along the line joining them. Use vector direction to determine attraction or repulsion; the force pair acts on different charges.
The principle of superposition says the net force is the vector sum of the forces from each other charge separately.

sections.heading: Electric field and potential
bullets: Electric field E=F/q_test; a positive test charge defines the field direction. For a point charge, E=kq/r² radially outward for positive q and inward for negative q.
Electric field lines originate on positive charge and terminate on negative charge; closer spacing represents stronger field. Lines do not cross.
Electric potential V is potential energy per unit charge. For a point charge V=kq/r, a scalar; potential differences are often easier to add than field vectors.
Electric potential energy for charge q at potential V is U=qV. A positive charge naturally accelerates toward lower potential energy; voltage is energy change per unit charge.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Separate field direction from force direction: a negative charge feels force opposite the electric field.
Use superposition with vector components for multiple charges.
Distinguish electric potential (scalar) from electric field (vector) and potential energy from voltage.

sections.heading: Current, resistance and electrical power
bullets: Current I=ΔQ/Δt is charge flow per time. Conventional current direction is the direction positive charge would move.
Ohm’s law for an ohmic element: V=IR. Resistance depends on material and geometry; it is not a universal constant for every device under all conditions.
Electrical power P=IV=I²R=V²/R for an ohmic resistor. Electrical energy transferred over time is E=Pt.

Series resistors carry the same current and have R_eq=ΣR. Parallel branches have the same voltage and 1/R_eq=Σ(1/R_i). Equivalent resistance is less than the smallest branch resistance for parallel positive resistors.

sections.heading: Circuit rules and magnetic effects
bullets: Kirchhoff’s junction rule expresses charge conservation: total current entering a junction equals total current leaving.
Kirchhoff’s loop rule expresses energy conservation: the algebraic sum of potential changes around a closed loop is zero. Choose loop direction and track rises and drops consistently.
A moving charge or current produces a magnetic field. Magnetic force on a moving charge is F=qv×B; magnitude |q|vB sin θ. Force is perpendicular to both velocity and field.
Magnetic flux Φ_B=BA cos θ for uniform field through a flat area, where θ is angle between the field and area normal. Flux changes when field, area or orientation changes.

sections.heading: Electromagnetic induction
bullets: Faraday’s law: induced emf magnitude is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux, |ε|=|ΔΦ_B/Δt| (for a coil, multiply by number of turns N).
Lenz’s law gives direction: induced current creates a magnetic field opposing the change in flux that produced it. ‘Opposes change’ is not necessarily ‘opposes the original field.’
Generators convert mechanical energy to electrical energy by changing flux; motors use magnetic forces on currents to produce motion; transformers change AC voltage through mutual induction.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Reduce a circuit step by step and track which elements share current or voltage.
For Kirchhoff problems, label assumed current directions; a negative solved value means the actual direction is opposite.
For induction, identify what changes the flux, then apply Lenz’s law to oppose that change.

sections.heading: Materials and diodes
bullets: Conductors have mobile charge carriers; insulators strongly restrict carrier motion; semiconductors have conductivity between these and can be controlled by impurities, temperature, light or electric fields.
Doping creates n-type material with electrons as majority carriers or p-type material with holes as majority carriers.

A p-n junction diode conducts readily under forward bias and strongly restricts current under reverse bias (up to breakdown). The conventional diode symbol and current direction should be read from anode toward cathode when forward biased.
Rectification uses diodes to convert alternating current into pulsating direct current; filtering can smooth the output.

sections.heading: Transistors and logic gates
bullets: A transistor uses a small control signal to regulate a larger current and can act as an amplifier or switch. Identify terminals and device type before analyzing a circuit.
Digital logic gates operate on binary inputs and outputs. AND is true only when all inputs are true; OR is true when at least one input is true; NOT reverses the input.
A truth table enumerates every input combination and gives the gate output. Combine gates one stage at a time when evaluating a logic circuit.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Explain how forward and reverse bias affect a diode and sketch qualitative current behavior.
Distinguish majority carriers in n-type and p-type materials.
Complete a truth table for a circuit by evaluating each gate in sequence.

topics.title: Physics across science, technology and society

sections.heading: Agriculture, environment and industry
bullets: Physics supports agriculture through measurement and sensing, irrigation and fluid flow, soil and moisture monitoring, climate observations, mechanization and energy use.
Environmental applications include tracking energy and matter, radiation and pollution measurement, remote sensing and understanding heat transfer and fluid circulation.
Industrial physics applies mechanics, materials, electricity, electronics, heat and measurement to manufacturing, process control, quality assurance and safety.
In application questions, identify the physical principle, the instrument or process that uses it, and the quantity measured or controlled.

sections.heading: Health sciences and archaeology
bullets: Medical imaging applies physical interactions: X-rays are attenuated by tissue, ultrasound uses reflected sound, and other imaging methods use electromagnetic or nuclear phenomena. Imaging methods differ in what signals they detect and their risks and limitations.
Radiation can be used for diagnosis and treatment; safe practice depends on dose control, shielding, distance, exposure time and appropriate procedures.

Archaeological and earth-science dating methods use measurable physical change over time, such as radioactive decay or accumulated signals. A method is chosen based on material, age range and assumptions.
Scientific dating estimates age from evidence and a model; it depends on calibration and whether the sample has remained suitably isolated.

sections.heading: Earth, space and power generation
bullets: Physics explains seismic and geophysical measurements, remote sensing, planetary motion and observations of Earth and space.
Power generation converts energy from sources such as flowing water, wind, sunlight, fuels or nuclear processes into electrical energy through physical mechanisms and engineered systems.
Compare energy technologies by source, conversion steps, efficiency, reliability, environmental effects and the scale at which energy is available.
Conservation of energy helps trace conversion losses: useful output is less than or equal to input, and efficiency η=(useful output energy or power)/(input energy or power)×100%.

sections.heading: Cross-cutting exam review
bullets: For each application, connect a named physics principle to a real measurement, device or process.
State benefits and limitations together; a technology’s usefulness depends on context, accuracy, cost, safety and environmental effects.
Use correct units and distinguish measured observations from conclusions inferred through a model.
